**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 2 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Answer FIVE questions, choosing AT LEAST TWO from each section. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Points : le sujet imprime les points de chaque partie (a) et (b), jamais le total de la question ; `points` de l'exercice est donc laissé vide. Les parties totalisent 20 pour chaque question (10+10, 10+10, 10+10, 10+10, 12+8, 12+8, 12+8, 8+12), conformément à « All questions carry equal marks ». Aucun écart constaté.

Sujet scanné (filigrane gcerevision.com en travers de la page ; sur la page de garde, le texte du verso apparaît en transparence, en miroir) : l'ensemble reste lisible. Titre, niveau (ADVANCED LEVEL), code 0725, session JUNE 2026 et durée (trois heures) vérifiés sur la page de garde. Le sujet ne compte que deux pages : page de garde, puis les huit questions (Section A : 1 à 4 ; Section B : 5 à 8) sur une seule page.

Défaut d'impression : à la question 5(b) la lettre « (b) » est maculée (« (ḅ) ») ; lue comme (b) d'après la séquence (a), (b). Le numéro « 2 » en en-tête de page de garde est imprimé de façon approximative (« Economics 2 »).

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont rédigés (niveau Advanced). Les exemples chiffrés (TVA au taux hypothétique de 20 %, chaîne cacao 100 000 / 160 000 / 250 000 / 320 000 FCFA, élasticité de -0,5) sont hypothétiques et recalculés avec Python ; le taux de 20 % n'est pas le taux légal camerounais. Aucune statistique réelle n'est avancée.

Figures : trois schémas produits avec matplotlib (Q2 fig-1 prix agricoles à demande inélastique, Q2 fig-2 stock régulateur, Q6 fig-1 encaisses d'activité et de spéculation). Ils illustrent les corrigés ; le sujet n'imprime aucune figure. Les courbes sont schématiques, sans échelle chiffrée.

questions.enonce_markdown: When will an increase in national income indicate an improvement in the standard of living for a country? (12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** **National income** is the total value of goods and services produced by the residents of a country in a year (measured as GDP or GNP). The **standard of living** is the level of material welfare of the people, that is, the quantity and quality of goods and services which the average person can enjoy. A rise in national income does not automatically mean a higher standard of living; it does so only when the following conditions are met.

1. **The increase is in real terms.** National income measured at current prices may rise only because of **inflation**. The increase must be adjusted by a price index (real national income). If money income rises by 8 per cent and prices rise by 10 per cent, real income, and the standard of living, falls.
2. **The increase is faster than population growth (a rise in real income per head).** Per capita income = $\dfrac{\text{national income}}{\text{population}}$. If population grows faster than national income, income per head falls and the average person is worse off. For example, if real national income grows by 3 per cent while population grows by 2 per cent, real income per head rises by about 1 per cent.
3. **The increase is fairly distributed.** If the extra income goes to a small rich group while the poor remain poor, average income rises but the standard of living of most people does not improve. Greater equality in the distribution of income and wealth means that more people benefit.
4. **The extra output consists of goods and services that satisfy the needs of the people.** A rise in consumer goods, food, housing, health and education improves the standard of living; but if the additional output consists of **military equipment**, prestige projects or capital goods only, there is no immediate improvement in consumption.
5. **The increase is not obtained at the expense of leisure and working conditions.** If people have to work longer hours, or in worse conditions, to produce the extra income, their welfare may not improve. A rise in income accompanied by shorter hours and more leisure is a clear improvement.
6. **The increase does not harm the environment and the quality of life.** If higher output is accompanied by pollution, deforestation, congestion and the depletion of natural resources, the quality of life may fall even though income rises. Social costs (noise, crime, stress, urban crowding) should be set against the gains.
7. **The extra income accrues to residents.** If a large share of the extra output is produced by **foreign-owned companies** and the profits are sent abroad, national income (GNP) rises less than output (GDP), and local people gain little. A rise that comes from a temporary boom in the price of an export (for example oil) may not last.
8. **The increase is accompanied by an improvement in the availability of public and social services,** such as health care, schools, clean water and security, which are not fully captured in the national income figure.
9. **The figures are accurate and include the informal sector.** Where much of the production in a subsistence or informal economy is not recorded, the rise in measured national income may be due to better recording rather than to extra output.
10. **The rise is sustainable and stable,** and not due to a temporary windfall, which could be followed by a fall.

**Conclusion.** An increase in national income indicates a better standard of living when it is **real**, exceeds the growth of **population**, is **widely shared**, takes the form of **useful goods and services**, and is obtained without loss of leisure and without damaging the environment.

questions.enonce_markdown: How can the problem of double counting be eliminated when measuring national income? (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** **Double counting** is the error of including the value of the same output more than once in the calculation of national income. It occurs when the value of **intermediate goods** (raw materials, components and services used up in production) is counted both when they are produced and again as part of the value of the final goods in which they are used.

**Example.** Suppose a farmer sells cocoa beans worth 100,000 FCFA to a processor, who sells chocolate paste worth 160,000 FCFA to a biscuit maker, who sells biscuits worth 250,000 FCFA to shops, which sell them to consumers for 320,000 FCFA. If we add all the sales values, we get $100{,}000 + 160{,}000 + 250{,}000 + 320{,}000 = 830{,}000$ FCFA, but the real value of the final output to consumers is only 320,000 FCFA. The extra 510,000 FCFA is double (in fact multiple) counting.

The problem is eliminated by the following methods.

1. **The final output (product) method.** Only the value of **final goods and services**, those sold to the final consumer or used for investment or export, is counted. Intermediate goods are left out. In the example, only the 320,000 FCFA is included.
2. **The value added method.** The value added at each stage of production, that is, the value of output minus the value of the intermediate inputs bought from other firms, is calculated and then added together: $100{,}000 + 60{,}000 + 90{,}000 + 70{,}000 = 320{,}000$ FCFA. This gives the same answer as the final-output method, since the total value added equals the value of the final product.
3. **The income method.** Instead of counting output, the incomes earned in production (wages, rent, interest and profit) are added together. Since the incomes are earned only once, there is no double counting; however transfer payments (pensions, unemployment benefits, gifts) must be excluded, because they do not arise from production.
4. **The expenditure method.** Only spending on **final** goods and services is counted: consumption, investment, government spending and net exports (exports minus imports). Purchases of intermediate goods by firms are not included, and imports are deducted.
5. **Excluding sales of second-hand goods and financial transactions.** The sale of second-hand goods and transfers of shares and bonds should be left out, as they do not represent new output; counting them would be double counting of goods already counted in the year they were produced.
6. **Careful classification of goods.** The statistician must decide whether each good is intermediate or final (for example, flour bought by a baker is intermediate; the same flour bought by a household is final), which requires a clear definition and good statistics.

**Conclusion.** Double counting is avoided by measuring only final output, or by adding value added at each stage, or by adding incomes (excluding transfer payments), or by counting expenditure on final goods and services only.
